---
title: "Research"
---

My research studies how health and reproductive policy shapes the health and economic well-being of women, children, and families. I focus on three connected questions: how policy changes the care women receive around pregnancy and who bears the consequences; how those changes carry forward to infants and the families who care for them; and how legal and regulatory pressure shapes the physicians who deliver care. I answer these questions with quasi-experimental designs and large administrative data, especially health insurance claims linked to provider records.

## Working Papers

::: {.card-soft style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;"}
### It Was Already Dobbs: Abortion Bans and Maternal Health

The Supreme Court's decision in *Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization* raised concerns that strict state abortion bans would worsen maternal health, especially for Medicaid-covered, Black, and Hispanic women. Using health insurance claims for commercially and Medicaid-insured pregnancies from 2020 to 2024, I compare states that enacted bans with states that protect abortion in a stacked difference-in-differences design. Because claims record each woman's health in the year before conception, I can separate whether bans changed *who* becomes pregnant from *what happens* to women once pregnant. I also test the channels through which harm was expected to travel: the management of miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy, care received out of state, and the supply of OB-GYNs.

<span class="pill-tag">Scheduled Presentation: SEA 2026</span>
:::

::: {.card-soft style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;"}
### First Do No Harm: The Labor Market Consequences of a Physician Disciplinary Record
with Colleen Carey and Amanda Agan

Using a novel dataset of 70,000 state medical board disciplinary actions across more than 40 states (2008–2023), we provide the first evidence on how State Medical Board discipline affects subsequent physician careers. Most disciplined physicians continue practicing—often in a new state and supplying fewer claims—evidence that can inform the optimal design of state oversight and disciplinary actions.

## Works in Progress

::: {.card-soft}
### Born After Dobbs: Abortion Bans, Prenatal Diagnosis, and the Prevalence of Congenital Conditions

Abortion bans may change which pregnancies continue after a serious prenatal diagnosis. I test whether bans raised the prevalence at birth of conditions usually detected during pregnancy, such as Down syndrome, relative to conditions that cannot be detected before birth, and follow affected infants through their first year of care.
:::

::: {.card-soft style="margin-top: 1.5rem;"}
### Hard to Concentrate: Prenatal Air Pollution and Childhood ADHD

Using medical claims for millions of children and Clean Air Act nonattainment designations that required states to reduce fine particulate pollution, I study whether exposure before birth raises the probability of an ADHD diagnosis later in childhood. Preliminary evidence shows that higher county air pollution is associated with more visits for ADHD, anxiety, and depression among children in the same year.
:::
